Minh Connors | Bloomberg | Getty Images Meta is slated to report third-quarter earnings after the bell on Wednesday, and investors will be looking for signs that the company's latest artificial intelligence efforts will bolster future sales. Here's what analysts polled by LSEG are expecting: Earnings per share : $5.75 Revenue : $63.2 billion It's been a big quarter for Mark Zuckerberg's company due to the initial success of the Muse AI personal assistant tool that debuted in September and shot to the top of Apple's iOS app store. That AI momentum helped Meta end September with its best month on Wall Street since 2022. Meta isn't the first to create a digital assistant that can organize people's email and scan the web for headphone deals, but the company's empire, which includes Facebook and Instagram, has helped introduce AI agents to the masses. At the same time, Meta and its AI chief Alexandr Wang have continued rolling out new foundation models and related updates at a speedy clip, including Muse Wonder , which was released last Monday. Wall Street will likely be monitoring for whether Meta plans to increase its data center-related capital expenditures, or capex, to further develop the underlying computing infrastructure needed to power AI agents and foundation models. The company revealed in July during its second-quarter earnings that it narrowed its 2026 capex guidance to come in between $130 billion and $145 billion, representing a $5 billion increase to the low end of its prior range. All that spending resulted in Meta's free cash flow in the period shrinking to $784 million from $8.55 billion in the same quarter a year earlier. Analysts expect Meta's capex to swell to $196.3 billion in 2027, according to FactSet. Meta's third-quarter daily active people, or DAP, is expected to come in at 3.65 billion, according to StreetAccount, almost flat from the prior quarter. That figure represents all of Meta's users across its family of apps like Facebook and Instagram. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images Analysts at Bank of America wrote in a note published Friday that they expect Meta to post a sales beat, with revenue of $63.8 billion, based in part on the firm's "solid ad checks" with brands and companies that helps determine the health of the digital ad market. The analysts don't expect Muse to contribute significantly to Meta's overall business for the rest of this year and 2027 and instead "will consume capacity w/o near-term revs.," meaning that the company's AI agent efforts will take some time to grow into something bigger. Morgan Stanley analysts agree that Meta's Muse AI agent initiatives won't generate big sales anytime soon, and while they said in a Sunday research note that they are "bullish," they "encourage investors to keep reasonable adoption rates in perspective." The analysts explained that it takes a long time for new technology habits and behaviors to normalize. In 2000, when the e-commerce boom was just five years deep, for instance, the analysts noted that online retail "only made up 4% of adj retail sales" while adding that "even ~30 years in ('26) it's still only 28%." — Jonathan Vanian 1 Hour Ago Meta sets the stage for hyperscaler earnings watch now VIDEO 4:39 04:39 AI capex cycle has 2-3 more years to run, says economist Access Middle East Meta will be the first hyperscaler to reveal quarterly financials during this tech earnings cycle, with Alphabet , Microsoft and Amazon slated to report next week. The four companies combined have called for roughly $730 billion in capital expenditures this year as they stock up on graphics processing units and AI systems and look to build massive data centers around the globe . Analysts polled by FactSet expect that number to hit around $1 trillion next year, led by Alphabet, which is projected to spend over $310 billion. The stepped up spending comes as interest rates soar and concerns intensify that AI revenue won't justify the costs. Alphabet and Microsoft are scheduled to report earnings next Wednesday, followed by Amazon on Thursday. — Jonathan Vanian 2 Hours Ago Meta’s legal headaches and state AG settlement watch now VIDEO 12:01 12:01 Watch CNBC's full interview with California AG Rob Bonta Squawk on the Street Meta's past quarter wasn't all AI agents and good vibes. The social media giant agreed in August to pay nearly $17 billion to settle a major lawsuit involving a group of state attorneys general, including California's Rob Bonta. The trial centered around allegations that Meta misled the public about the true scope of child mental health related harms caused by certain design elements of apps like Facebook and Instagram , including recommendation algorithms. Meta's state AG settlement could cause the company to miss on third-quarter earnings per share due to the related $10 billion legal charge that "the street has not yet accounted for," Wolfe Research analysts wrote in a Monday note. The company still faces numerous personal injury claims and a separate federal case involving a group of nationwide school districts that also focus on allegations that apps like Instagram have had detrimental effects on the well being of children. — Jonathan Vanian

The penalty comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data. A New Mexico district court judge said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. Brendan McDermid | Reuters Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had over 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion. "The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico district court judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing. The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full. CNBC has reached out to Meta for comment on the penalty order. Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September. In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg-led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices. Judge Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. "Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said. Former New Mexico state Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Raúl Torrez oversaw the related trial. Torrez also led his state's child-safety related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance. Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal. headlines.article_text: Intel hits construction milestone at delayed Ohio chip fab Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Intel’s first Ohio fab was originally expected to begin production in 2025. Operations are now targeted for 2030 or 2031. Intel says construction and tool installation are underway at its next Arizona fab, with operations expected by the end of 2028. Reported discussions with SK Hynix could bring memory production to the Ohio site, but no deal has been confirmed. In this article INTC Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Intel announced on Oct. 20, 2026, that crews have installed the first major structural truss at its new chip fabrication plant in New Albany, Ohio. Courtesy: Intel Intel has hit a milestone in the construction of its massive chip fabrication plant in New Albany, Ohio, that's running at least five years behind schedule, a delay that's coincided with soaring demand for advanced chips. On Wednesday, Intel announced that crews have installed the first major structural truss in Ohio, which means the next part of the construction has finally begun. "This represents another significant step toward expanded U.S. leading-edge semiconductor capacity," Intel Foundry head Naga Chandrasekaran wrote in a post on the company's website on Wednesday. Intel still needs customers to make the investment pay off. In September, reports surfaced that the world's leading maker of high-bandwidth memory, SK Hynix , could team up with Intel in Ohio to lease some foundry space to make memory chips at the new site. Neither company would confirm any plans. When Intel first announced the Ohio factory in 2022, it was expected to start delivering chips in 2025. Intel pushed back that timeline, now aiming to finish construction in 2030. A second Ohio fab is also planned for completion in 2031 at the site, just northeast of Columbus. The delay reflects a broader recalibration of Intel's foundry ambitions under CEO Lip-Bu Tan. The Ohio factory is only one piece of Intel's ambitious build-out to start making chips for outside customers that began under former CEO Pat Gelsinger. When Tan took the helm in 2025, his turnaround strategy was more cautious, choosing to wait for customer demand before forging ahead with ambitious chip fab plans. Still, by late 2025, Intel was in high-volume production at its Arizona chip fab , producing its most advanced 18A chips. On Wednesday, Chandrasekaran also announced that operations at its next fab in Arizona are expected to begin by the end of 2028. But Intel has yet to land a major external customer for those 18A chips coming out of Arizona. Instead, Intel is using them to make its own processors for devices. Once a dominant force in the chip manufacturing landscape, Intel hit major delays with its 7- and 10-nanometer nodes, triggering the stock's worst year ever in 2024. Customers have been reluctant to commit again since. Now, Intel's window of opportunity may have arrived alongside record demand for AI, as leading chip manufacturer Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. can't make chips fast enough. Even for the biggest chipmakers like Nvidia , Advanced Micro Devices , Apple and Broadcom , "competition is extremely fierce," to get space on TSMC's factory lines, according to Mizuho Securities analyst Jordan Klein. Intel could offer customers an alternative source for chip production, according to TechInsights analyst Dan Hutcheson. "People want a second source to be able to twist TSMC's arm and keep them honest on pricing," Hutcheson said. "All the big ones have been testing there." headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: SPCX, META, SMCI, ROIV Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. Roivant Sciences — Shares rose more than 4% after the company's immune-modifying pill Lisraya reached its primary efficacy goals in two Phase 3 trials for non-infectious uveitis, a disease of the eye. Bloom Energy — The fuel cell company jumped more than 6% as traders snapped up shares ahead of Thursday's third-quarter report. The FactSet consensus sees earnings coming in at 69 cents per share on revenue of $1.07 billion. Wolfe Research dubbed the company a "recent outperformer" in its preview of clean energy earnings, saying "demand signal continues to build, beat and raise potential." Bitcoin-linked stocks — Bitcoin jumped more than 2% to trade above $84,000 as investors flocked to risk assets. A raft of crypto-related stocks leapt alongside it, with Strategy gaining 7% and bitcoin miner MARA Holdings rising more than 3%. Riot Platforms advanced 2%. Alphabet — Shares of the tech giant slipped 2% after OpenAI said that its models will be available for developers via Google's cloud. The move follows years of competition between OpenAI and Alphabet, and it means the ChatGPT maker will have its models available on all three of the major U.S. cloud companies. Meta Platforms — The social media giant jumped 2% ahead of quarterly results due after the bell Wednesday. Muse, the company's artificial intelligence model, will likely be a key focal point after its closely watched rollout this fall. SpaceX — Shares gained 10% after the Elon Musk-led rocket company reported a 161% jump in third-quarter revenue to $14.58 billion. Musk also said that SpaceX and Tesla , his automaker, have formed special committees to discuss a potential merger. Tesla shares were up 3%. Telecom company EchoStar , which owns a stake in SpaceX, saw shares rise 8%. Space stocks — Other aerospace companies were higher following SpaceX's earnings jump. Rocket Lab rose 4%, while Firefly Aerospace jumped 5%. Netflix — Shares of Netflix fell almost 5% after the streaming giant narrowed its 2026 full-year forecast . The streaming giant now sees revenue at $51.1 billion, reflecting a 13% year-over-year increase and landing at the low-end of its earlier guidance range of $51 billion to $51.4 billion. AT & T — The telecommunications company slid 6% despite reporting an earnings and revenue beat in its third-quarter financial report. AT & T also hiked its full-year earnings guidance, though it reiterated capital expenditures that came in slightly above expectations, according to FactSet. Capital One Financial — The lender and credit card issuer gained about 4%. Third-quarter net income reached $3.5 billion, or $5.61 per share, up from $3.2 billion, or $4.83 a share in the year-earlier period. United Airlines — The Chicago-based carrier jumped 5%. While third-quarter results missed on the top and bottom lines, the company pointed out that passengers are still booking even as fares have risen. Passenger counts are up more than 2% from the year-ago period, while domestic passenger unit revenue gained 14.5% in that timeframe. Super Micro Computer — Shares rallied 9% after the data center server company hiked its fiscal first-quarter revenue outlook. Super Micro sees revenue for the period between $18.5 billion and $19.5 billion, up from a previous range of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion. Dell Technologies , Hewlett Packard Enterprise — Super Micro's server competitors Dell and HPE were also higher on the news of the company's guidance update. Dell jumped almost 5%, while HPE rose 3%. Danaher — Shares lost 3% after the life sciences and diagnostics innovator reported a slight revenue miss in its third-quarter earnings report. Revenue came in at $6.55 billion, compared the $6.56 billion FactSet consensus estimate. Adjusted earnings, however, beat estimates, and the company raised its full-year guidance for the metric. — CNBC's Nick Wells, Darla Mercado, Deena Zaidi, Fred Imbert and Scott Schnipper contributed reporting.

headlines.article_text: Tesla (TSLA) Q3 2026 earnings report Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Tesla's earnings report comes a day after SpaceX announced better-than-expected profit and revenue. On the earnings call, CEO Elon Musk said the boards of both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a potential merger. Tesla shares are down 14% so far this year, underperforming all of the company's tech megacap peers. In this article TSLA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Tech billionaire and Tesla founder Elon Musk at a meeting. Johannes Neudecker | Picture Alliance | Getty Images On SpaceX's earnings call late Tuesday, CEO Elon Musk , who also runs Tesla , took a break from talking about financial results to tell investors that it would be a "good idea" to merge his two companies, and said the boards at both have formed special committees to discuss a possible tie-up. Musk will be back in public after market close on Wednesday, this time to discuss Tesla earnings. Here's what Wall Street is expecting, according to estimates from analysts polled by LSEG: Earnings per share: 43 cents estimated Revenue: $27.9 billion estimated Should Tesla fail to top expectations, the company would see a slight decrease in revenue from $28.1 billion a year earlier. Tesla has recorded double-digit growth in each of the two prior quarters, but revenue dropped in three of four quarters in 2025, as Chinese EV makers such as BYD and Xiaomi gained popularity in Asia and Europe with affordable and innovative EVs. Tesla was also hit last year by the end of a federal EV tax credit. Earlier this month, Tesla reported vehicle deliveries for the third quarter of 486,532, about 2% below the year-ago number. Deliveries are the closest approximation of sales reported by Tesla but are not precisely defined in its shareholder communications. While Tesla still counts on auto sales for the bulk of its revenue, Musk sees the company's future in robotaxis and humanoid robots. That's putting the focus on capital expenditures, which are expected to top $25 billion this year, based on a prior forecast, up from about $8.5 billion in 2025. Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster nearly a decade after first revealing a next-generation version of its original electric sports ​car, at a launch event in Waco, Texas, Oct. 15, 2026. In this still image taken from a handout video the Roadster comes to a landing using rocket thrusters. Tesla | Via Reuters One of Tesla's big investments is in a semiconductor factory that it's building with SpaceX and Intel in Grimes County, Texas. That partnership with SpaceX along with other areas of overlap, including work on Tesla's recently announced Roadster refresh, fueled intensifying speculation that Musk's companies were on the verge of combining in what would be a historic transaction. "I feel like I'm tap dancing through a minefield," Musk said on the SpaceX earnings call, responding to a question about a potential merger. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said. "But at the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this." On the Tesla side, that means needing a 50% vote of all shares, which is "quite a high hurdle," he said. Musk pointed to the company's potential to cooperate on AI software, chip design, Terafab and robotics. Tesla is already using Grok AI technology, developed by SpaceX, to power AI assistants in customer cars, and to help control the company's Optimus humanoid robots now in development. Tesla's stock price is down 14% this year, after rallying on Wednesday, underperforming all of its megacap tech peers. SpaceX went public in June, and is up from its $150 IPO price after its post-earnings pop. Tesla CFO Vaibhav Taneja told investors on the company's last earnings call in July that automotive margins had been challenged this year by rising interest rates and energy costs. But he also touted growing revenue from Full Self-Driving (Supervised), sometimes referred to as FSD, the partially automated driving system Tesla sells for $99 per month. FSD doesn't make Tesla vehicles safe to use without a human driver, and the company markets the system as Assisted Driving in Europe. Taneja said Tesla reached close to 1.5 million paid FSD customers globally as of the end of June. Investors submitted questions online ahead of Wednesday's call, and one of the top-voted requests was for updates on FSD and when it could become "unsupervised," making customers' vehicles fully automated and safe to use like a robotaxi. Shareholders also want to hear an update on Tesla's Cybercab, a bronze two-seater designed for use as a robotaxi, but not yet sold to individuals. Tesla is testing the Cybercab, and has deployed driverless vehicles in a limited U.S. fleet. But the company still lags far behind Alphabet's Waymo in the U.S., and Baidu's Apollo Go in China. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:47 06:47 Brad Gerstner on Trump Accounts: One of the most successful changes to our social contract in 100 years Squawk Box Elon Musk said earlier this week that he plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year, and CEO of Altimeter Capital Brad Gerstner said Wednesday that the stock donations would come via Trump Accounts . If it happens, that donation of $10.5 billion worth of shares is just the beginning, according to Gerstner, the founder of Invest America and an architect of Trump Accounts, the new tax-deferred investing accounts for kids. "Elon is the tip of the iceberg," Gerstner told CNBC's "Squawk Box" in an exclusive interview on Wednesday. "This is the most giving country on the planet," he said. "I told the president, I think I can raise $100 billion over the course of the next 12 months to sponsor all of the kids in America." In addition to Musk, Gerstner said he had also talked to "every major tech CEO and founder." A $100-billion fundraising target would represent about one-sixth of all U.S. charitable giving. "The Treasury targeted this carve-out at mega-donors and large philanthropic foundations, such as the Dells, who made a multibillion-dollar charitable pledge," said Adam Bergman, founder of IRA Financial and a tax attorney based in Miami. "They range from small to mega," he said. "We do have mega donors in the nine-digit range, you know, bunches of them." Future Trump Account expansion "As @TrumpAccounts continues to grow we look forward to more philanthropists joining the movement and helping children across America jumpstart their financial future," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in an X post Monday . The latest Trump Account comments come weeks after the Treasury Department auto-enrolled more than 60 million children . Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts , are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number. Children born from 2025 through 2028 may also claim a one-time $ 1,000 pilot program contribution from the Treasury. Gerstner also said Wednesday that there is a push to expand access to the accounts to all U.S. citizens under age 40. "Why not pull forward 20 years of IRAs? We can create all of those today," he said. "So if Elon says then, I want to give to everyone under 40, or OpenAI says I want to give to everyone under 40, there's a vehicle, there's a vessel that they can start compounding in….those are the types of things we are working on." In addition to more than 70 million children under 18 in the U.S., about 90 million U.S. citizens are between 18 and 40 years of age, according to CNBC's analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data. However, expanding Trump Accounts to Americans under age 40 would require a legislative change from Congress. In an X post on Tuesday , Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, called the proposed expansion a "game-changer," and said he would "lead the bill in the Senate to make it happen." Gerstner told CNBC on Wednesday that expanding the Trump Account age limit is "wildly popular" among Congressional Democrats and Republicans. But it's unclear whether the proposal has the legislative backing needed to become law.
